A comprehensive understanding of the life history of the Southern greater glider (Petauroides volans) requires detailed physiological and developmental data obtained under controlled conditions. Basal metabolic rate measurements, for instance, have been recorded in resting, post-absorptive individuals at a body temperature of 35.4 °C [T = 35.4 °C], revealing a maximal oxygen consumption of 432.8 milliliters per hour [JOi = 432.8 milliliters per hour]. This relatively low metabolic output, when scaled against the species' adult mass, aligns with the energy-conserving strategy typical of arboreal folivores. The gestation period is notably brief for a marsupial of this size, lasting only 13 days [tg = 13 days] under the same thermal regime of 35.4 °C, after which the altricial neonate emerges to begin its protracted developmental journey in the pouch at a temperature of 35.4 °C [T = 35.4 °C].

At parturition, the newborn joey is remarkably undeveloped, with a recorded wet weight at birth of merely 0.273 grams [Wwb = 0.273 grams]. This diminutive size necessitates an extended period of intense maternal investment within the protective environment of the pouch. The dependent young remains continuously attached to a teat for several months, undergoing most of its organogenesis during this sheltered phase. The transition to nutritional independence is marked by weaning, which, under optimal thermal conditions maintained at 35.4 °C [T = 35.4 °C], occurs at 176 days after birth [tx = 176 days after birth]. At this point, the juvenile has attained a wet weight at weaning of approximately 150 grams [Wwx = approximately 150 grams], representing a substantial increase from its birth mass but still only a fraction of the ultimate adult size.

Juvenile gliders continue to grow and develop after leaving the pouch, gradually refining their locomotor and foraging skills within the maternal home range. The protracted period of maternal care is a hallmark of this species, reflecting the challenges of subsisting on a low-energy diet of eucalypt leaves. Under the stable thermal regime of 35.4 °C [T = 35.4 °C], the trajectory toward reproductive maturity is a slow one for females, as the time since birth at puberty is 639 days [tp = 639 days]. This delay in the onset of gonadal activity is consistent with a life-history strategy that prioritizes achieving a sufficiently large body frame before expending energy on reproduction, a common pattern among arboreal marsupials that face high metabolic constraints.

Once sexually mature, the breeding adult enters a reproductive schedule characterized by a very low intrinsic rate of increase. This is primarily governed by the maximum reproductive rate, which results in just a single litter per year [F_R_i = single litter per year] at a body temperature of 35.4 °C [T = 35.4 °C]. This annual output is among the lowest for any mammal of comparable body size, punctuated by the fact that females typically produce only a single offspring per litter [N_R_i = single offspring per litter]. The combination of a long gestation, an extended period of pouch life, and a prolonged dependency phase precludes the possibility of more frequent breeding, tightly linking the population's growth potential to adult survival and the availability of high-quality forage.

The ultimate expression of this slow-paced life history is the species' considerable longevity. Maximum lifespan in the wild has been estimated at approximately 12.8 years [am = approximately 12.8 years] when measured at the stable body temperature of 35.4 °C [T = 35.4 °C]. This extended lifespan is a critical demographic buffer against the species' low fecundity, allowing individuals multiple reproductive opportunities across their lifetime. Furthermore, the maximum adult body mass, or ultimate wet weight, for a healthy female is typically around 1350 grams [Wwi = around 1350 grams], though males are notably smaller and can be significantly lighter. This sexual dimorphism, coupled with the species' low metabolic rate and high longevity, paints a picture of a K-selected specialist finely adapted to the unpredictable resources of its sclerophyll forest habitat.
